To better understand your condition, have you noticed any specific patterns to the rash, such as it appearing in waves or spreading from your neck down?

speaker: Patient
text: 11-year-old girl. The patient has been experiencing a mildly pruritic rash on her trunk and extremities for 2 days. One week ago, she developed symptoms of low-grade fever, rhinorrhea, and headache. A facial rash appeared 4 days later, sparing the perioral area.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for those details; the timing of the facial rash sparing the mouth is very specific. Given your history of fever and runny nose followed by this rash, did you or anyone close to you have a similar illness recently? REQUEST TEST: Complete_Blood_Count.

text: RESULTS: Complete_Blood_Count: WBC - Normal, Hemoglobin - Normal, Platelets - Slightly elevated

speaker: Doctor
text: The complete blood count shows normal white and red blood cells with slightly elevated platelets, which is a common reactive finding. Given the classic progression of fever, rhinorrhea, and the specific description of a facial rash sparing the nose, have you noticed any joint pain or significant swelling in your hands and knees?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Mildly pruritic rash on trunk and extremities. I also have Low-grade fever, Rhinorrhea, Headache, Facial rash not involving the perioral skin.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Roseola Infantum (Exanthem Subitum).

The clinical picture of high fever followed by defervescence and the appearance of a pruritic maculopapular rash sparing the face and perioral area is classic for Roseola, likely caused by Human Herpesvirus 6 or 7. Given the specific history and normal CBC, no further testing is required; the condition is self-limiting and typically resolves within 24 to 48 hours.
